burp in Latin

burp

ructō, ructāre · ructus, ructūs m.

Ancient LatinQuotationsComposed phrasesDraft
  • ructō, ructāre — burp, belch classical (Plaut. Ps. 1300; Cic. Phil. 2.63; Juv. 3.107)
  • ructus, ructūs m. — a burp classical (Plaut. Ps. 1301; Cic. Fam. 9.22.5)
  • Quid, lubet? pergin' ructāre in ōs mihi? — Suāvis ructus mihi est. Sīc sine, Simō. — What, you feel like it? Will you keep burping in my face? — My burp is a sweet one. Leave me be, Simo. (Plaut. Ps. 1300–1301)
  • in Pompōniō cōnsulārī poētā nōn ructāsse — of Pomponius, the consular poet, that he never burped (Plin. NH 7.78)
  • Nōlī inter cēnam ructāre. — Don’t burp at the table. composed

See also: hiccup.
